property_summary: For every caller address, after calling airDrop through an address that reports support via Bank, the reference contract always leaves tokenBalance(caller) either unchanged if it was non-zero (hasNoBalance prevents mint) or increased by 20 if it was zero; the mutant that removes hasNoBalance allows callers with existing non-zero balances to gain an additional +20, violating that rule.

For any caller address that initially has a non-zero tokenBalance, the reference contract C prevents airDrop from increasing that caller's tokenBalance (it remains unchanged); the mutant (which removed the hasNoBalance guard) allows some such callers to have their balance increased by 20, violating this rule.

For any caller address that already has a non-zero tokenBalance, calling airDrop (via an address that answers supportsToken() correctly) does not change that caller's tokenBalance in the reference C, while the mutant (which removed the hasNoBalance guard) can increase an existing non-zero balance by 20.

For every caller address that initially has a non-zero tokenBalance, calling airDrop (through an address that reports supportsToken()) never changes that caller's tokenBalance in the reference C; the mutant that removed the hasNoBalance check can increase such existing non-zero balances by 20.

For any pair (caller, reporter) where reporter.supportsToken() returns the expected hash, if reporter != caller then calling airDrop through reporter may affect reporter's tokenBalance in mutant but in reference the airDrop only ever increases tokenBalance[msg.sender] (the caller) and never changes balances of other addresses; therefore the reference preserves tokenBalance of any third-party address k != caller, while the mutant can change some k != caller when misused — so assert that for any fuzzed caller and third-party k (k != caller) a call to airDrop by caller routed through a reporter does not change tokenBalance(k).

After any single successful airDrop call by any caller, the tokenBalance of that caller increases by 20 and remains callable subsequently (i.e., airDrop does not permanently block future calls for other callers); the mutant that never resets the reentrancy lock can permanently block future airDrop calls and thus can make tokenBalance observations diverge.

For any caller address that reports support for the exact string "Nu Token" via Bank(msg.sender).supportsToken(), calling airDrop increases that caller's tokenBalance by 20; the mutant changes the compared string to "NuToken" so callers that correctly report keccak256("Nu Token") will be rejected and airDrop will not increase their balance.

For any caller address a that currently has zero tokenBalance, calling airDrop from a will always increase tokenBalance(a) by 20 (reference); the mutant that requires tokenBalance>0 prevents zero-balance callers from receiving the airdrop, breaking this rule for some inputs.

For any caller with zero prior tokenBalance and who is recognized by supportsToken, calling airDrop always increases their tokenBalance by exactly 20 in the reference; the mutant that adds 40 breaks this by sometimes yielding a balance increase != 20.

For any caller who currently has zero tokenBalance and whose supportsToken() matches, a single successful airDrop call increases their tokenBalance by exactly 20 in the reference contract; the mutant that adds 40 will cause some such callers to end up with a balance != 20.

For any caller address that initially has tokenBalance == 0 and whose supportsToken() matches, a successful single airDrop call increases tokenBalance by exactly 20 in the reference contract; the mutant that adds 40 will make the final tokenBalance sometimes differ from 20.

For any caller address, after a successful airDrop call the reference contract always leaves its reentrancy guard unlocked allowing subsequent calls (i.e., _locked resets so airDrop can be called twice by the same caller), whereas the mutant that fails to reset _locked breaks this by permanently locking after the first call for some caller inputs.

For any caller address that initially has zero tokenBalance and whose supportsToken() matches, calling airDrop once succeeds and leaves the contract's reentrancy guard unlocked so a second immediate airDrop call from the same caller also succeeds (i.e., two consecutive airDrop calls by the same admissible caller both return/complete); the mutant that fails to reset _locked causes the second call to revert/fail for some callers, breaking this rule.

For any admissible caller that initially has zero tokenBalance and whose supportsToken() returns the expected bytes32, calling airDrop once succeeds and leaves the contract in a state where the public _locked getter (inherited) is false (i.e., the reentrancy guard is reset); the mutant that fails to reset _locked leaves _locked == true after the call for some caller, breaking this rule.

For any caller address with initial tokenBalance <= 0, calling airDrop always increases that caller's tokenBalance by exactly 20 in the reference; the mutant that relaxes hasNoBalance to <=10 allows some callers with small positive balances (1..10) to also call airDrop, so their post-call balance differs from the reference (reference would have refused them and left balance unchanged).

For any caller address and its initial tokenBalance, the correct contract C allows airDrop only when the caller's balance is exactly 0 (so after a successful call the getter tokenBalance(caller) == 20), whereas the mutant that relaxes hasNoBalance to <=10 permits callers with small positive balances (1..10) to also succeed—thus the invariant 'if initial balance != 0 then airDrop must revert (leaving balance unchanged)' holds for reference but is broken by the mutant for some inputs.

For any caller address, the reference contract only permits airDrop when the caller's tokenBalance is exactly 0 (so a successful call sets tokenBalance[caller] == 20); the mutant relaxing hasNoBalance to <=10 allows callers with small positive balances (1..10) to also succeed, breaking that rule for some inputs.

For every caller and starting balance, the reference contract only allows airDrop to succeed when the caller's tokenBalance is exactly 0 (so after a successful call tokenBalance[caller] == 20); the mutant that relaxes hasNoBalance to <=10 permits callers with small positive balances (1..10) to also succeed, violating that rule for some inputs.

For any caller address and its initial tokenBalance, the reference contract only allows airDrop to succeed when the caller's tokenBalance is exactly 0 (so a successful call results in tokenBalance[caller] == 20); the mutant that relaxes hasNoBalance to <= 10 allows callers with small positive balances (1..10) to also succeed, violating this invariant for some inputs.
